9 Leadership Lessons From Nick Saban
Monte Burke
Contributor
Aug 4, 2015, 09:23am EDT
Share to Facebook
Share to Twitter
Share to Linkedin
My new book, Saban: The Making of a Coach, is officially out today. I spent the better part of the last year-and-a-half working on it full-time, interviewing more than 250 of Saban’s friends, colleagues, former players, college roommates, rivals and golfing buddies. The idea behind the book was fairly simple: I wanted to discover what has influenced and motivated the man who has won four national titles and is one of the most successful sports coaches of all time.
One central question the book addresses is this: What makes Nick Saban such an effective leader? Here are a few answers to that question from the book.
1) Adapt and Adjust: Saban’s father—and first football coach —was one of his most significant influences. “Big Nick” demanded of his son an impossible-to-achieve perfection. When Saban threw a touchdown pass for his Pop Warner team, his father/coach offered him critiques—his footwork was poor, his spiral wasn’t tight—instead of congratulations. As one of Saban’s childhood friends told me: “His father just drove him unmercifully. I always thought [Saban] had two options growing up: to become a great success or go crazy.” Saban opted for the former, adjusting to his father’s expectations rather than crumbling in the face of them. He learned to embrace and love the “doing”—the actual steps taken in pursuit of perfection—rather than focusing on the unattainable goal. In a significant way, this adaptation of behavior became one of the pillars of what’s now known as Saban’s “Process.”
2) Stick to Your Guns: At 11:10 am on December 31, 1981, Saban was fired for the first and only time in his career, as the secondary coach at Ohio State. One of the primary reasons Saban was fired: He and the Ohio State head coach, Earle Bruce, vehemently disagreed about what type of cornerbacks and safeties they should be playing and recruiting. Saban saw the writing on the wall, early on: Football was becoming a passing-dominated game. Saban wanted quicker, more athletic safeties who could play man-to-man defense and better defend the pass. Bruce was of the old school tradition that held the belief that safeties should be big run-stoppers. Saban lost this battle but won the war. He quickly landed on his feet with another job, and was eventually proven correct about the transformation of the game. Bruce never coached big-time college football again after being let go during the 1987 season.
3) Dress for Success: It sounds simple and sort of Esquire -y, right? But it has helped Saban. Early in his assistant coaching career at Navy, Saban was the only coach on the team who wore a suit around campus and in meetings. He was dressing “up.” He continues to do so to this day. He has a tailor in Miami who makes the suits he wears on recruiting trips. The bespoke suits make an impression, especially on the parents of recruits. “A lot of these parents aren’t making a lot of money, and they see this guy come in, just off the plane, wearing a suit, a guy with a plan,” says one of Saban’s former Alabama assistants. “They don’t see many people like that. What they saw with him was a man who was blunt, straightforward, and successful.”
4) Take Control of Your Job Interviews: Saban won jobs at both Michigan State and Louisiana State during his initial interviews. Terry Denbow, a former Michigan State spokesperson who attended the school’s first interview with Saban, said: “It was the best interview I’ve ever seen and I’ve seen a lot of them.” At Saban’s LSU interview, one of the trustees present said: “He was interviewing us hard, and we were interviewing him less hard.”
5) Stay Focused: One of Terry Saban’s favorite stories about her husband goes something like this: One evening while at MSU, Saban met a friend at a bar to talk football. As the two men talked, a man robbed the place. Saban never once looked up. Some moments later, as he stood up to leave, Saban finally noticed an unsettled air about the bar. He asked the bartender what was up. The bartender stared at him incredulously. “You didn’t notice that we just got robbed?” he asked.
6) Be Relentless—and Prepared—While Recruiting Talent: Saban once sat in the metal stands on a frigid day and watched an entire soccer game just to get in a word with LSU recruit, Jacob Hester, who was moonlighting as his high school’s goalkeeper. Saban once knew the brand of chewing gum that a certain recruit preferred. He frequently comments on the drapes and other furnishings in a recruit’s home, which endears him to the mothers. He tells recruits exactly what he has in mind for them on the team, providing them with a detailed vision of their future.
7) Surround Yourself With the Right People: Saban’s agent, Jimmy Sexton, rubs some people the wrong way. But he’s clearly “best in biz” in college football. Saban’s offensive coordinator at Alabama, Lane Kiffin, also rubs some people the wrong way, but he is an excellent coordinator. Saban’s wife, Terry, is pretty much universally loved, and her strong, protective hand has helped lead her husband through both the peaks and the valleys.
8) Use Your Leverage: Saban, with the considerable help of Sexton, has used his leverage to get contract extensions and raises, especially after winning national titles or attracting interest from other teams. Some have found this unseemly. Saban has also caught much grief over the years for his job-hopping. But in every move—from MSU to LSU, from LSU to the Miami Dolphins, from the Dolphins to Alabama—he has put himself in a better position and made more money. And he’s proven time and time again that he’s worth the money.
9) Get the Details Right: Saban’s “Process” is all about focusing on the journey, and not the destination, and about doing the right thing the right way all the time. That focus manifests itself in many different ways, some big and some small. One example: An Alabama insider remembers watching a game coached by Saban’s predecessor at Alabama, Mike Shula. “After a game, the Alabama sideline was a mess, with crushed water cups and tape all over the ground. After Saban’s first game [at Alabama], I just happened to look at the sideline. It was pristine.”

Why is Nick Saban such a successful coach? ESPN's Louis Riddick gives his take
ALABAMA
Why is Nick Saban such a successful coach? ESPN's Louis Riddick gives his take
Michael Wayne Bratton| 4 years ago
After winning yet another National Championship at Alabama, Nick Saban continues to stake his claim as the greatest coach in the history of college football.
So what is it that makes Saban so successful? Why does he stand out from all the other outstanding coaches in the country? Aside from simply pointing to the number of championships he’s racked up over time, ESPN NFL analyst Louis Riddick offered up his insight as to what separates Saban and his mentor and friend Bill Belichick, who most would argue is the best NFL coach of all time.
Not only does Riddick study the workings of both coaches for a living for ESPN, he played for them both in Cleveland — Riddick was a defensive back in the NFL for nearly a decade. Riddick also isn’t your typical analyst, he’s so well thought of around the NFL he’s been interviewed for general manager openings and is in discussion to take over for Jon Gruden’s role as the lead analyst on Monday Night Football.
During a recent appearance on the Sports Illustrated Media Podcast, hosted by Richard Deitsch, Riddick was asked what exactly it is about Saban that makes him stand out from other coaches.
“First and foremost, he’s an expert at the game of football. He understands all the positions, how they all work together. He could coach any position if it was necessary. Bill Belichick the same,” Riddick said on the podcast. “If one day, the quarterback coach or the tight end coach or the inside linebacker coach for some reason couldn’t coach for a couple of weeks, a couple games, these guys could step right in and coach that position equal to or better than their position coach. They have an overall working knowledge of the game that is freaking incredible. I’ve seen it, I’ve seen Bill do it, I know Nick can do it.”
Riddick went a step further and discussed what it’s like playing for Saban in the defensive backfield and how the coach helps to get the absolute best out of every player he can.
“In specifics to playing defensive back, which is Nick’s specific expertise, the nuance of the game from what you need to know pre-snap as far as what your opponent is going to do — based on their alignment and their personnel — he gives those pitches to you in a way that makes sense to you and ways you can apply functionally once the ball is snapped,” Riddick continued. “The mental preparation, this goes for Bill too — when I talk about this stuff, they both do it — they give you the information in a way you can use and apply once the game starts going better than anyone I’ve ever been around.
“Post-snap, they drill you and hold you to such a high level of accountability for doing it, fundamentally the way they teach it to you, they direct those things over and over to the point where it becomes a part of your muscle memory and you wind up playing the game fundamentally at a level that is even higher than you thought you could play it at. And the reason you do it is because they won’t let you not do it, because if you don’t do it the way they want you to, you won’t play for them. In college, you will sit the bench, you’ll wind up transferring or having your ego destroyed because you thought you were some hot-shot five-star but he won’t put you on the field because you won’t do it the way he wants.”
Simply put, according to Riddick, Saban’s greatness comes down to one key — accountability. While other coaches talk about it, the ESPN analyst says Saban and Belichick demand it from everyone in their organization.
“The accountability is really the thing that separates them from other coaches I’ve been around,” Riddick concluded.
